title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Financial Accounting First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Every business, from a roadside provision store to a big company, must know how much money it has, how much it owes, and whether it is making a profit. Financial Accounting is the subject that teaches you how to record, sort and report this information so that owners, banks, the tax office and workers can all trust it.

In First Term you learn what book-keeping and accounting are, the rules of behaviour (ethics) every accountant follows, the double entry system that is the heart of accounting, how to write ledger accounts and journals, the basic ideas (concepts) behind all accounts, and how to keep an analytical cash book.

Read each unit slowly. Accounting is learned by doing: copy every worked example in your notebook and then try the practice work yourself. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Book-keeping and Accounting: Meanings and Differences
summary: What book-keeping is, what accounting is, examples of each, and four or more differences between them.

p: Book-keeping is the process of recording financial transactions in a systematic and time-order (chronological) way in the books of account. A transaction is any exchange that has a money value, such as buying goods, selling goods or paying rent.
Features of book-keeping: it deals with recording only; the work is routine and repeated; it is clerical in nature; it does not need special professional skills; it is concerned with HOW to record.
Examples of book-keeping activities: recording sales in the sales book; recording purchases in the purchases book; posting entries to the ledger; keeping the cash book; filing vouchers and invoices.

Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating financial information so that the people who use it can make informed judgments and decisions. It includes book-keeping and goes further: it summarises, analyses and interprets the records.
Features of accounting: it includes book-keeping plus analysis and interpretation; it needs professional judgment; it is concerned with WHY and WHAT DOES IT MEAN.
Examples of accounting activities: preparing financial statements; analysing profitability; calculating ratios; giving financial advice; auditing accounts (checking that accounts are true and fair).

title: Importance of Accounting
summary: Ten reasons why accounting matters to owners, managers, banks, the government and the law.

p: A business owner may say, 'I do not need accounting; I know how much money I have.' That thinking is wrong, because money in the pocket does not show what is owed, what is owned, or whether the business earned a profit. Accounting is important for these reasons.
1. Keeping systematic records: all transactions are recorded properly, past records are easy to find and information is not lost.
2. Measuring profit or loss: it shows whether the business is making a profit and whether it is worth continuing.
3. Showing the financial position: it shows what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and what the owner has put in (capital), which shows the net worth.
4. Helping decision making: it gives information for planning and for choosing between alternatives, such as whether to buy a van or hire one.
5. Comparison: this year can be compared with earlier years and with other businesses, so trends can be seen.
6. Meeting legal requirements: companies must keep accounts by law, the tax authorities need them, and regulators require them.
7. Control: it helps to detect errors and fraud, prevents theft of money and goods, and makes people accountable.
8. Evidence in court: properly kept records can be used as evidence in disputes and legal cases.
9. Valuing the business: records help to decide the worth of a business for sale, or when a partner joins or leaves.
10. Getting loans: banks ask for financial statements to see whether a business can repay.

Users include the owner, managers, workers, banks and other lenders, suppliers (who may sell on credit), customers, the Federal Inland Revenue Service and state tax bodies, and investors. Each wants different information from the same accounts.

title: Ethics of Accounting: Professional Conduct
summary: What accounting ethics are, why they matter, and the five principles of professional conduct with examples.

p: Accounting ethics are the moral principles and standards that guide the behaviour of accountants and make sure that financial reports are honest. In Nigeria, professional accountants belong to bodies such as the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN) and the Association of National Accountants of Nigeria (ANAN), which set the rules.

Why ethics matter: they keep public trust; they protect the good name of the profession; they protect the interests of everyone who uses the accounts; they make financial information accurate; and they prevent fraud and the changing of figures to deceive people.
Professional conduct means the standard of behaviour expected from accounting professionals. The main principles are these.
1. Integrity: being honest and straightforward, not falsifying records, and admitting mistakes. Example: not increasing profit figures just to please the owner.
2. Objectivity: being fair and unbiased, not favouring any party, and letting facts guide decisions. Example: an auditor who does not favour a friend's company.
3. Professional competence: keeping knowledge and skills up to date and doing work properly. Example: attending training on new tax laws.
4. Professional behaviour: obeying laws and rules and avoiding actions that bring the profession into disrepute. Example: refusing to take part in tax evasion.
5. Due care: working carefully and diligently, meeting deadlines and checking one's work. Example: reviewing financial statements thoroughly before signing.

Professional bodies usually list five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care (written together as one), confidentiality, and professional behaviour. Your notes treat confidentiality separately (next unit) and split competence and due care into two. Both ways of grouping teach the same ideas.

title: Confidentiality, Transparency, Integrity and Ethical Dilemmas
summary: Keeping client information private, being open in reporting, having strong moral principles, and solving common ethical problems.

p: Confidentiality means keeping client information private and not telling it to anyone without proper authority.
Do not disclose: the client's financial information, business secrets, personal details or trade information.

When disclosure is allowed: when the law requires it (for example a court order); when the client gives permission; to professional regulatory bodies; and when it is needed to protect the public interest.

Good examples: not discussing a client's profits with friends; not giving a client list to competitors; keeping salary information private. Bad examples: telling others about a company's money problems; using client information for personal gain.
Breaking confidentiality can lead to loss of licence, legal action, damage to reputation, loss of clients, and fines.

Transparency means being open, honest and clear in all financial reporting. It needs full disclosure (reporting all important information and explaining the accounting policies used), clarity (clear, understandable presentation that does not mislead) and accuracy (correct figures that show the true position).

Examples of transparency: disclosing all liabilities, not just some; explaining unusual transactions; reporting losses honestly. Examples of the opposite: hiding bad debts; creating false invoices; leaving out large expenses.
Benefits: it builds trust, helps better investment decisions, prevents fraud, improves the reputation of the company and supports good governance.

Integrity means being honest and having strong moral principles in all professional dealings. Its parts are: honesty (telling the truth); ethical behaviour (doing what is right, not just what is legal); consistency (keeping the same standard for everyone); and moral courage (standing up for what is right and speaking out against wrong).

Threats to integrity: pressure from management, personal gain, fear of losing a job or client, lack of knowledge and a weak ethical culture. How to protect integrity: know the professional standards; ask for guidance when unsure; write down your decisions; report unethical behaviour; and put the public interest first.

title: Double Entry: Meaning and Types of Accounts
summary: The double entry system, why every debit has a credit, and the three types of account: personal, real and nominal.

p: The double entry system is a method of recording transactions in which every transaction affects at least two accounts: one account is debited and another is credited, with equal amounts. The rule is: for every debit there must be a corresponding credit.

The method was described in 1494 by the Italian monk Luca Pacioli, who is often called the 'Father of Accounting'. (He wrote down the method that merchants in Venice were already using; he did not invent it.)
Example: goods bought for cash, ₦5,000. Purchases account is debited ₦5,000 (goods come in) and Cash account is credited ₦5,000 (cash goes out).

Benefits: a complete record of transactions; errors can be found (if debits do not equal credits); it shows cause and effect; it allows a trial balance to be prepared; and it gives a check on accuracy.
Personal accounts are accounts of persons: individuals, firms and companies. Examples: John's account, ABC Limited account, creditors and debtors. Rule: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real accounts are accounts of assets and property. Examples: land, building, furniture, machinery, stock (goods in hand). Rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

Nominal accounts are accounts of expenses, losses, incomes and gains. Expenses and losses include salaries, rent, electricity and bad debts. Incomes and gains include sales, commission received, interest received and discount received. Rule: debit all expenses and losses; credit all incomes and gains.

title: Golden Rules, Debit and Credit, and Simple Entries
summary: The golden rules of accounting, which side increases each type of account, the accounting equation and five worked entries.

p: Study the table.

A memory aid: for personal accounts, debit the receiver and credit the giver. For real accounts, debit what comes in and credit what goes out. For nominal accounts, debit expenses and losses and credit incomes and gains.

Debit (Dr) is the left side of an account. It increases assets, expenses and losses, and it decreases liabilities, capital and income. Credit (Cr) is the right side. It increases liabilities, capital and income, and it decreases assets, expenses and losses.
The accounting equation is: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. It must always balance. The diagram shows the effect of debit and credit on each part.

img.alt: The accounting equation Assets = Capital + Liabilities with small boxes under each part showing whether debit or credit increases or decreases it
img.cap: The accounting equation and the effect of debit and credit.

p: Example 1: Started business with cash ₦50,000. Cash (an asset) comes in, so debit Cash ₦50,000. The owner has put in capital, so credit Capital ₦50,000.
Example 2: Bought goods for cash ₦10,000. Purchases are an expense, so debit Purchases ₦10,000. Cash goes out, so credit Cash ₦10,000.
Example 3: Sold goods for cash ₦15,000. Cash comes in, so debit Cash ₦15,000. Sales are income, so credit Sales ₦15,000.
Example 4: Bought furniture from ABC Ltd on credit ₦20,000. Furniture comes in, so debit Furniture ₦20,000. ABC Ltd is the giver, so credit ABC Ltd ₦20,000.
Example 5: Paid salary ₦5,000 in cash. Salary is an expense, so debit Salary ₦5,000. Cash goes out, so credit Cash ₦5,000.

Before writing any entry, ask three questions. (1) Which two accounts are affected? (2) What type of account is each? (3) Which golden rule applies to each, so which is debited and which is credited? Write the debit first.

title: Ledger Accounts in T Format
summary: What a ledger is, the T-account layout, and the five steps for recording transactions in the ledger.

p: The ledger is the book that contains all the accounts of a business. Each account has its own page (or its own T). Entries are first written in the books of original entry (journals and the cash book) and are then posted (copied) into the ledger accounts.

A T-account looks like the letter T. The name of the account is written at the top. The left side is the debit (Dr) side and the right side is the credit (Cr) side. Each side has columns for the date, the details (the name of the other account involved) and the amount in naira (₦).

img.alt: A cash account drawn in T format with debit side on the left and credit side on the right, showing entries, balance c/d, totals and balance b/d
img.cap: A cash account in T format, with the balance carried down and brought down.

p: 1. Identify the accounts involved. 2. Classify each as personal, real or nominal. 3. Apply the golden rules. 4. Record the amount on the correct side of each account, writing the name of the OTHER account in the details column. 5. Balance the accounts at the end of the period.

Jan 1: started business with cash ₦100,000. Jan 3: bought goods for cash ₦30,000. Jan 5: sold goods for cash ₦45,000. Jan 8: paid rent ₦5,000. Jan 10: bought furniture ₦20,000. Jan 15: received commission ₦3,000. Jan 20: paid salaries ₦8,000. Jan 25: withdrew cash for personal use ₦10,000.
The Cash account shows all of these because cash is involved each time.

Each of the other accounts has just one entry. Capital: credit ₦100,000 (Cash). Purchases: debit ₦30,000. Sales: credit ₦45,000. Rent: debit ₦5,000. Furniture: debit ₦20,000. Commission received: credit ₦3,000. Salaries: debit ₦8,000. Drawings: debit ₦10,000. Cash is debited when money comes in and credited when money goes out.

title: Balancing Accounts: A Worked Example
summary: How to balance a ledger account (c/d and b/d), which accounts have debit and credit balances, and a complete worked exercise.

p: 1. Add up both sides (debit and credit) separately. 2. Find the difference. 3. Write the difference on the side with the smaller total as 'Balance c/d' (carried down). 4. Now both sides add up to the same total; write the total on both sides at the same level. 5. Draw a double line under the totals to show that the account is closed. 6. Bring the balance down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' (brought down) to start the next period.

Rules: assets and expenses normally have debit balances. Liabilities, capital and income normally have credit balances. If the debit side is bigger, the balance is a debit balance; if the credit side is bigger, it is a credit balance.

Record these transactions in ledger accounts and balance them. 1 Mar: started business with ₦200,000 cash. 5 Mar: bought goods for cash ₦80,000. 8 Mar: sold goods for cash ₦100,000. 12 Mar: paid rent ₦10,000. 15 Mar: bought equipment from Ade on credit ₦50,000. 18 Mar: received a bank loan ₦150,000. 22 Mar: paid Ade ₦30,000. 25 Mar: paid electricity ₦5,000. 28 Mar: sold goods for cash ₦75,000. 31 Mar: paid salaries ₦20,000.

Cash account: the debits are capital ₦200,000, sales ₦100,000, loan ₦150,000 and sales ₦75,000, which add up to ₦525,000. The credits are purchases ₦80,000, rent ₦10,000, Ade ₦30,000, electricity ₦5,000 and salaries ₦20,000, which add up to ₦145,000. The difference is ₦380,000, the closing balance.
Ade's account: the equipment of ₦50,000 was bought on credit, so Ade is credited ₦50,000. The ₦30,000 payment is a debit. The balance still owed is ₦20,000, a credit balance (we owe Ade).

Balances of the other accounts: Capital ₦200,000 credit; Purchases ₦80,000 debit; Sales ₦175,000 credit; Rent ₦10,000 debit; Equipment ₦50,000 debit; Bank loan ₦150,000 credit; Electricity ₦5,000 debit; Salaries ₦20,000 debit; Ade ₦20,000 credit.

Add the debit balances: cash 380,000 + purchases 80,000 + rent 10,000 + equipment 50,000 + electricity 5,000 + salaries 20,000 = ₦545,000. Add the credit balances: capital 200,000 + sales 175,000 + loan 150,000 + Ade 20,000 = ₦545,000. They agree, which shows that the double entry is correct. A list like this is called a trial balance, which you will meet in Second Term.
